messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Somchai had always been the sort of man who relied on precision, routine, and the careful parsing of details; for decades he had worked as a cybersecurity analyst, comfortable tracing patterns others missed. After his wife died, he lived alone, carrying the quietness of his apartment in a way that made ordinary days feel more exposed. The trauma that altered that steadiness had occurred years earlier, when his only child became gravely ill as a baby and was rushed through repeated examinations and procedures in a hospital that smelled sharply of antiseptic. He remembers standing under harsh fluorescent lights while nurses moved quickly around a tiny body, and he remembers how the baby’s cries, the sight of medical equipment, and the invisible but unmistakable hospital odor became fused in his mind with the terrifying possibility that his child might die. Even now, a medical appointment can bring that night back with such force that Somchai feels his chest tighten and his body go on alert before he has time to think. The same happens when he sees a pregnant woman, a newborn in a waiting room, or even a photo of childbirth on television; these reminders do not stay small or symbolic, but immediately wake the old fear, horror, guilt, and shame he has come to expect.

What troubles Somchai most is how quickly those reminders pull him into the experience itself. He says the memory plays “like a film” that starts on its own and will not stop, and when it comes he feels as though the danger is happening right now rather than belonging to the past. The hospital smell in particular can make him feel abruptly back in that corridor, and the old scenes return with all their force: the baby under the lights, the hurried voices, his own helplessness. In those moments he has had flashes of acting as if the crisis were still unfolding, scanning for the next sound or movement that might signal something was going wrong again. He tries to explain the event to his daughter and finds himself losing the thread, stopping mid-sentence because the sequence breaks apart and the images take over. That difficulty describing it has made him feel even more alone with it, as though the experience cannot be properly held in words.

Over time, Somchai began to dread the bodily surge that followed these reminders. The fear and guilt rush in together, and he becomes intensely aware of his own breathing, pulse, and tension, interpreting every wave of reaction as proof that the old catastrophe is still near. If he has to pass through a hospital lobby, sit in a clinic, or even stand near the smell of antiseptic at a pharmacy, he can feel his body respond before he can reason with himself. He avoids unnecessary medical appointments whenever possible and has started to rely on phone calls or written notes instead of going in person, because being in those settings can set off the whole sequence all over again. He also avoids conversations about pregnancy or babies, leaving family gatherings briefly when relatives talk about newborn grandchildren. These small decisions have narrowed his life: he is less willing to accompany friends to the doctor, and he has become increasingly isolated, preferring the safety of his apartment and his work-from-home setup.

Yet the memory itself also keeps feeding the very cues that summon it. When Somchai is alone, the film-like replay grows more vivid, and once it is active he becomes primed to notice anything that resembles the original hospital scene. A television commercial with a baby, a distant disinfectant smell from a medical supply cabinet, or a routine checkup notice in the mail can suddenly carry the weight of that earlier terror. The more often the memory breaks through, the more alert he becomes to the world for signs that might bring it back, and the smaller his life has become around that anticipation. In his cybersecurity work, he now keeps his office door closed and declines tasks that require him to escort staff to the building’s clinic, because the environment there is too closely linked to the old experience. The pandemic-era habit of smelling hand sanitizer in hallways has become, for him, another small but sharp reminder that can set everything in motion.

He finally sought help after a recent dental visit, when the antiseptic smell in the office hit him so suddenly that he felt as if he were back at the hospital beside his infant child. He left before the appointment was finished and sat in his car shaking, ashamed that at 75 he could still be so overwhelmed by something from so long ago. What he hopes for now is not to forget his child’s illness, but to be able to remember it without being dragged into it, and to stop living as though every hospital corridor, every baby, and every trace of antiseptic might open the same terrifying door again.
